escalate.g: To increase (something) in extent or intensity; to intensify or step up.

escape.e: From Middle English escapen, from Anglo-Norman and Old Northern French escaper ( = Old French eschaper, modern French échapper), from Vulgar Latin *excappāre (“to escape a garment, get out of one's clothing”, literally “to free oneself from one's cape”), from Latin ex- (“out”) + Late Latin cappa (“cape, cloak”).
escape.g: To get free; to free oneself.

escapee.g: Someone who has become free through escaping imprisonment.

eschew.e: From Middle English eschewen, from Anglo-Norman eschiver, (third-person present eschiu), from Frankish *skiuhijan (“to dread, shun, avoid”); thus a doublet of skew. For the pronunciation with /ʃ/, compare the development of marshal from Middle English marschal (/marsˈt͡ʃaːl/) or Middle English myssheve, variant of myschef (“hardship”).
eschew.g: To avoid; to shun, to shy away from.

escort.e: Borrowed from French escorte, itself borrowed from Italian scorta.
escort.g: A group of people or vehicles, generally armed, who go with a person or people of importance to safeguard them on a journey or mission.

espousal.e: From Middle English espousal, espousaille, from Old French espousailles, from Latin sponsalia (“a betrothal”), neuter plural of sponsalis, from spōnsus (“one betrothed, a spouse”); see spouse. By surface analysis, espouse + -al.

espouse.e: From Middle English espousen, borrowed from Old French espouser, from Latin spōnsāre (frequentative of spondeō), from Proto-Indo-European *spend-.

espy.e: From Middle English aspien, espien (“to make covert observations of (a person or place) with hostile intent, to spy on; to seek to discover by spying; to act as a spy; to catch sight of, see; to look over, observe; to wait in ambush, to ambush; to plot against; to look for, seek to find; to inquire or look into, investigate; to discover, find”).
espy.g: To find out or observe (someone or something, especially if not easy to see) by spying or looking; to catch sight of; to see; to spot.

espy.e: From Middle English aspie, espie (“covert investigation or observation, scouting, spying; information obtained through spying; secret and treacherous plan, plot; treachery; a scout or spy”), from Anglo-Norman espie, Old French espie, from espier (verb): see further at etymology 1.
espy.g: An act of finding out or observing by spying or looking; an espial or espying.

essence.e: From Middle English essence, from Middle French essence, from Latin essentia (“the being or essence of a thing”), from an artificial formation of esse (“to be”), to translate Ancient Greek οὐσία (ousía, “being”), from ὤν (ṓn), present participle of εἰμί (eimí, “to be, exist”).
essence.g: The inherent nature of a thing or idea.

essential.e: From Late Latin essentiālis, from Latin essentia (“being, essence”).

establish.e: From Middle English establissen, from Old French establiss-, stem of some of the conjugated forms of establir (modern French établir), from Latin stabiliō, stabilīre, from stabilis (“firm, steady, stable”).
establish.g: To make stable or firm; to confirm.

establishment.e: From Middle English *establishment, stablishment, stablisshement, from Old French establissement (modern French établissement), from the verb establir. By surface analysis, establish + -ment.
establishment.g: The act or process of establishing; a ratifying or ordaining; settlement; confirmation.

estate.e: From Middle English estat, from Anglo-Norman estat and Old French estat (French: état), from Latin status.
estate.g: The collective property and liabilities of someone, especially a deceased person.

esteem.e: First at end of 16th century; borrowed from Middle French estimer, borrowed from Latin aestimō.
esteem.g: Assessment, estimation, or regard; especially; favourable estimation or regard.

estimate.e: From Middle English estimat, borrowed from Latin aestimātus (“valuing, estimate”, only used in the ablative singular: "aestimātū..." (in valuing...)), from aestimō + -tus (“action noun-forming suffix”).
estimate.g: A rough calculation or assessment of the value, size, or cost of something.

estimate.e: From Latin aestimātus (“estimated”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and Etymology 2 for more. Originally used as the past participle of estimate; compare generate or communicate.

estimation.e: From Middle English estimacioun, estimacion, from Old French estimacion, from Latin aestimatio. Morphologically estimate + -ion.
estimation.g: The process of making an estimate.

estrange.e: From Old French estranger (“to treat as a stranger”), from Latin extraneus (“foreigner, stranger”) (from which also strange, stranger).
estrange.g: To cause to feel less close or friendly; alienate. To cease contact with (particularly of a family member or spouse, especially in form estr
